name: The Sickles Witness Tree

location.address: United States Avenue near the Trostle Farm, Gettysburg National Military Park, Pennsylvania
location.neighbourhood: Auto tour stop 11, Trostle Farm, north side of United States Avenue

access: Free, within Gettysburg National Military Park; on public land directly beside United States Avenue at auto tour stop 11, reachable on foot or by pulling off the road.
transport: No public transit; the park is a short drive from downtown Gettysburg, PA. Roadside parking near the Trostle Farm.
verify_notes: A swamp white oak standing at the Trostle Farm on the afternoon of 2 July 1863, when Union Major General Daniel Sickles gathered under it (one of the few shaded spots on that part of the field) to confer with his officers before advancing his corps to the Peach Orchard, a move that reshaped the second day's fighting. A period sketch by artist Charles Reed shows the tree as it stood that day, which is the documentary evidence for its presence at the battle (the standard NPS-style basis for a 'witness tree' claim: identifiable in a dated period image or record). Two independent sources (Gettysburg Daily, a long-running local history site, and Civil War Cycling's witness-tree survey) both confirm it alive today; Civil War Cycling's 2025-updated survey lists this Trostle Farm tree as alive with no damage notes, in contrast to several other witness trees on the same list now dead or removed. Age given as roughly 175-220 years by an independent tree-marker source (Waymarking), consistent with a tree already substantial in 1863 (163 years before this pass). Girth not found this pass. Location precision: confirmed via a plotted GPS coordinate from a dedicated historic-tree marker page, matching the address description (Trostle Farm, US Ave, tour stop 11) given by every other source.

name: The Copse of Trees
species: Chestnut Oak and others (Quercus prinus and mixed oaks)
age_estimate: not documented; the current trees postdate the 1863 battle

location.address: The Angle, Hancock Avenue, Gettysburg National Military Park, Pennsylvania
location.neighbourhood: About 0.4 mile south of town, west side of Hancock Avenue, within the stone-walled Angle, at the base of the High Water Mark monument

access: Free, within Gettysburg National Military Park; a short walk from Hancock Avenue on the paved battlefield paths, enclosed by a low iron fence installed in 1887 to protect it from souvenir hunters.
transport: No public transit; the park is a short drive from downtown Gettysburg, PA. Roadside parking on Hancock Avenue.
verify_notes: HONESTY FLAG, important: NPS states plainly on its own page for this exact site that none of the trees standing inside the fence today date to 1863. In 1863 this was a small clump of bushes and trees used by Confederate planners as the visual target for Pickett's Charge on 3 July 1863; reaching it (the closest the attack got to breaking the Union line) is what gives the spot its name, the High Water Mark. So this is NOT a witness-tree entry in the age sense; it qualifies, if at all, purely on historical significance as a landmark ensemble people already travel to stand at (per CLAUDE.md's ensemble test: compact, famous for being exactly that, one obvious place to stand -- comparable to the precedent of a famous replanting keeping its page on the strength of the event rather than the trunk's age). Today it is roughly half a dozen large trees, mostly chestnut oak, fenced since 1887. The story, if written, must say plainly that these are not 1863 survivors. Species mix and count are approximate (stonesentinels and other sources do not give a precise count or full species list); no girth or age found; alive and actively maintained as a monument site, no death/removal concerns.

name: General Gibbon's Walnut Tree

location.address: Hancock Avenue, Cemetery Ridge, Gettysburg National Military Park, Pennsylvania
location.neighbourhood: Center of the Union line on Cemetery Ridge, beside Weir's Battery position, just off Hancock Avenue

access: Free, within Gettysburg National Military Park; on public land directly beside Hancock Avenue on Cemetery Ridge, reachable on foot.
transport: No public transit; short drive from downtown Gettysburg, PA. Roadside parking along Hancock Avenue.
verify_notes: A black walnut on Cemetery Ridge at the center of the Union line, where Confederate troops broke through briefly during Pickett's Charge on 3 July 1863. Local legend, repeated by multiple sources, holds that Union Brig. Gen. John Gibbon was wounded near this tree during the assault; treat the wounding-at-this-exact-tree detail as legend/local tradition rather than a documented fact, but the tree's presence on the ridge during the battle is the underlying witness-tree claim and is corroborated by American Battlefield Trust (a national nonprofit, independent of the dedicated witness-tree site) alongside gettysburgwitnesstrees.com. Age estimate (200+ years, meaning it was already a mature tree by 1863) and girth (2023 measurement: 112in circumference/284cm, up from an estimated ~26in diameter in 1906) come from gettysburgwitnesstrees.com's own measurement record; this is the best-sourced girth figure found in this pass. The tree lost the top of its main trunk in a 2021 storm but survives and reportedly still fruits every summer (per the same 2023-dated source), which is stronger and more recent alive-evidence than a 2008 newspaper piece (Gettysburg Daily) that worried the tree was failing. Also notable: it is the sole survivor of a 1916-1917 park programme that filled 33 witness trees' trunk cavities with concrete, visible today through a crevice at the base.

name: The Devil's Den Witness Tree

location.address: Sickles Avenue, above Devil's Den, Gettysburg National Military Park, Pennsylvania
location.neighbourhood: On a sharp curve on high ground above Devil's Den, across from the Smith's 4th New York Independent Battery monument

access: Free, within Gettysburg National Military Park; on public land directly beside Sickles Avenue overlooking Devil's Den, reachable on foot.
transport: No public transit; short drive from downtown Gettysburg, PA. Roadside parking nearby.
verify_notes: A white oak standing on the high ground overlooking Devil's Den, with what both sources call a 'balcony view' over Houck's Ridge, the Slaughter Pen and the western slope of Little Round Top: on 2 July 1863 this spot looked down on the opening clash of Longstreet's assault, about 2,400 Union troops under Birney against 5,500 Confederates under Hood. It was a seedling or sapling at the time of the battle (estimated 8 to 8.5 inch diameter in 1863 against 51.6 inches / 162in circumference measured in 2023), so it is a genuine witness but a young one by this project's usual standard, not an ancient tree; the story should be honest that its interest is what it overlooked, not its age. Identification as a period witness rests on an 1899 published photograph showing the tree already established on the same spot, per gettysburgwitnesstrees.com. Two independent sources (American Battlefield Trust, a national nonprofit, and the dedicated gettysburgwitnesstrees.com survey) agree on species, location and that it is alive today, with matching coordinates.
